title: Crocodiles Balance Sticks on Their Snouts, and Only in Nesting Season

scenes.text: Some crocodiles lie still with sticks balanced on their snouts.
It looks like an accident. But in India, a scientist watched mugger crocodiles hold the pose for hours, right beside nesting birds.
In Louisiana, his team then watched alligators for a year. The sticks showed up near bird colonies, and mostly from March to May.
That's when egrets build nests, and sticks run so short that birds fight each other over them.
An egret wades in for the perfect twig. The log underneath it has teeth.
It's the first tool use ever reported in a reptile, and the first predator known to time its bait to its prey's calendar.

description:
Mugger crocodiles in India and American alligators in Louisiana lie in the shallows with small sticks balanced across their snouts, and nest-building birds that come for the sticks get eaten.
In a year of observations at four Louisiana sites, alligators displayed sticks mainly near bird rookeries and mainly from March to May, when egrets are building nests and sticks are scarce. The 2013 study called it the first report of tool use by any reptile, and the first known predator to time a lure to its prey's season.
Smart hunter or lucky log: what do you think?
